children: The key issue for energy markets is whether the current shock remains an inflationary force or starts to slow down activity, says Claudio Galimberti from Rystad Energy. "The Fed, the ECB and the Bank of Japan are all signaling they will not let energy-driven inflation become embedded in wages and prices," the chief economist says. "But raising rates adds a second restraint on growth through higher borrowing costs, bond yields and eventually weaker corporate earnings and household demand." Now, focus shifts to the Trump-Xi summit on Thursday, which could offer important clues on how quickly the market's supply deficit might widen or ease. Any signal on secondary sanctions against buyers of Iranian oil, or on whether China is prepared to adjust its purchases of Iranian crude, could materially alter the global supply outlook, Galimberti says. (giulia.petroni@wsj.com)
